prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realisation of optical lattice clocks, based on magic-wavelength trapping of many atoms, which brought optical frequency measurement to the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged: one part, B046, Katori and Ye. What the citation recognises that the 2005 comb prize and the 2012 prize on single quantum systems did not is the magic-wavelength lattice, in which thousands of neutral atoms are held with the lattice light shift cancelled, so that the statistics of an ensemble are combined with the small systematic shifts of a trapped system. Katori proposed it and demonstrated the first strontium clock, and the Ye group's record accuracy and stability, with agreement between independent clocks and between species at the 10^-18 level, made it a new measuring instrument. It has since reproduced across JILA, RIKEN/Tokyo, PTB, NIST and SYRTE, and it resolves gravitational redshift over millimetres and gives new limits on constants and dark matter. Both parts of the credit are physical ideas and realisations, not an engineering race. The round-1 exchange has also removed what I regarded as the strongest objection (see the factual correction below).
statement.case_against: The honest reservations are these. First, the fundamental-physics output so far consists of limits and demonstrations rather than discoveries, as Kroll and Danielsson say, so a critic can call this an instrument prize. I accept the label but note that the committee has rewarded new ways of observing nature before, and the lattice clock does open a regime of measurement that was not accessible with single ions or comb-referenced clocks. Second, Katori's proposal, Takamoto's first demonstration, Lemonde's early lattice work and the Ludlow and Bloom clocks are real contributions; a two-name cap leaves out people, and the priority history is partly from memory. Third, B038 has the cleaner conceptual novelty and a new class of matter, and I cannot dismiss that argument. Its credit gap (Bernevig, Hughes, Zhang, and the 3D work) is what keeps me from ranking it first, but I would not regard a B038 outcome as a mistake.

responses.point: Kroll recalls that the 2005 laureates were Glauber, Hall and Hansch, and that Ye, as a postdoc in Hall's group, was not a laureate, and asks that this be checked before the overlap argument is used.
responses.response: You are right and I withdraw my own statement in round 1 that Ye shares the 2005 prize. As I recall it, the 2005 prize went to Glauber for optical coherence and to Hall and Hansch for the comb, and Ye was not a laureate. I would suggest the committee treat that as the working record, and verify it in the archive before the final vote. This matters because it removes the argument that this would be a second prize for one person, though it does not remove the argument about a prize on an adjacent chain. I would also ask you to state your Hall-group connection formally. A declaration seems enough to me, because the science and the credit of Katori and Ye do not depend on your judgment of the comb, but the committee should record it and not leave it to be inferred.

responses.point: Olsson wants the committee to see the omission of Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang stated openly if B038 goes forward, and asks whether the lattice clock should wait for the SI redefinition of the second.
responses.response: On waiting, I still say no: the performance is verified in many laboratories and the legal definition of the second is a metrology-body timetable that does not change the physics. If anything, the redefinition will be built on this work, so recognising it now is consistent. On B038, I agree the committee cannot treat the BHZ proposal as a footnote, and the point you make is fair, that the omission has to be written into the discussion and not left to the reader. I am glad that you would take it seriously if the condensed-matter colleagues defend the trio. I note that Eriksson's reply, that the first observation and the symmetry-based concept are what the citation centres on, is a defensible position, and that is why B038 is my first alternative and no longer a candidate I rank last.

responses.point: Lindroth treats the 2005 and 2012 prizes as neighbouring ground rather than the same invention, and asks us to word the citation around the lattice-clock invention, with theory and experiment agreeing quantitatively.
responses.response: I agree, and I would take your wording one step further and require that the citation name the lattice explicitly, not just 'optical clocks'. Otherwise the committee invites the comparison with the single-ion clocks of the 2012 prize and with the comb itself. I also share your caution that the dispute with Lemonde and Takamoto should be answered in the record: Katori's proposal and first demonstration are in the invention, and the Ye group's record accuracy and stability are the realisation, which is why I want exactly these two names. Where I might differ from you is that I would not add a third name, because the three-person limit would then force a choice among Lemonde, Takamoto and Ludlow, none of whom has a claim that clearly outranks the others.

responses.point: Eriksson argues that time-reversal-invariant Z2 insulators are a distinct discovery from the 2016 topological-phase prize, and that the 2D quantum spin Hall effect is the cleaner core, and asks how wide the citation should be.
responses.response: I find your argument about 2016 persuasive as physics: the 2016 prize was about topological invariants in quantum Hall states and defects and phase transitions, while the Z2 class is a symmetry-protected phase with its own materials consequences. That reduces the overlap objection from my side, and it is a point I could not judge on my own. On width, I would keep the citation to the two-dimensional quantum spin Hall effect and the Z2 prediction and its first observation, and I would say in the committee's discussion that the 3D work and the BHZ proposal are acknowledged and excluded by choice. I still end up with B046 as the cleaner configuration, because it has no such gap to defend, but I now regard the choice as a close one and not as a clear win.

responses.point: Danielsson holds that a verified prediction of a new class of matter is rated above a precision-measurement record, and that the discoveries enabled by clocks are so far demonstrations rather than findings.
responses.response: I agree with your point about the discoveries, and I would not rest my case on constants drift or dark matter, where the output is limits. My case is that a regime of measurement has been opened and verified: clocks at the 10^-18 level agree between laboratories and between atomic species, and redshift is resolved over a millimetre in a single lattice. That is a physical observation, not only a promise. Your kind of discovery is clearer in B038, and I do not dismiss it. But I weigh attribution and maturity more heavily than you do at the end of the process, and B046 has the cleaner credit and nothing about its interpretation still being debated.

uncertainties: Whether the archive confirms my recollection that Ye was not a 2005 laureate; the committee should check this before the final vote, since my round-1 statement was wrong if so.
Whether Katori and Ye are the right two names, given Takamoto, Lemonde, Ludlow and Hinkley; all priority history is from memory and has not been checked against the primary papers.
Whether B038 is the better prize if the committee gives conceptual novelty more weight than attribution; I cannot judge Kane-Mele versus BHZ priority from my own field.

Whether circuit QED (B006) should be held until a later year; I regard the strong-coupling physics as stronger than the processor-platform case, and its credit among Blais, Girvin, Schoelkopf and Wallraff is not settled.
statement.conflict_note: I direct the Wallenberg Centre for Quantum Technology, work with superconducting-circuit groups at Chalmers and have proximity to the circuit QED community (B006) and to the 2025 laureates, so I would recuse myself from any discussion or vote on B006 and would defer on B033 and B009. B006 is only a secondary alternative in my position now and I would ask that it be treated in my absence if it comes up. I have no link to Katori or Ye apparent from my profile, and I note that Kroll has declared a link to the Ye group through John Hall's laboratory, which I think is a matter for declaration and not for recusal.
